title: Rain recency gave no clear warmth slope change in four eastern US frog-call samples in 2001-2015
abstract: We tested whether days since rain changed the link between survey-night warmth and a frog calling index. We used 6,573 NAAMP runs on 689 routes in two eastern US regions and two periods in 2001-2015. The index was the mean number of four fixed species heard per stop. Models controlled route-year, route-observer, season, wind and curved weather terms. The change in the 5 C warmth slope between one and seven days since rain ranged from -0.008 to +0.038 species per stop. All four 98.75 percent route-cluster intervals crossed zero. Two-way route and year intervals and added state season curves did not change that result. Removing route-year control gave one positive interval, which did not repeat under the main model. Incomplete rain reports, chosen survey nights, sparse dry-night support and unobserved calling activity limit inference. The result does not show that weather has no effect. It is not a test of true species richness, population change, climate trends or air pollution. Code, aggregate results, exact source hashes, a figure and fit checks are included.

display.caption: Rain recency and warmth slope contrasts in four NAAMP samples. All adjusted intervals include zero. Blue intervals use route clusters. Orange intervals use route and year clusters.

citations.reason: Uses the same public data source and region definitions. Extends the weather observation question to rain recency and survey-night warmth. Raw survey records overlap; this is not independent confirmation of its spring timing result.
